title: I was excited by Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons until the protagonist pulled out a sword
summary: Can't we just stick to the magic?
body: Considering only eight minutes of it were shown at Gamescom's Opening Night Live, I went on a real journey with Warlock: Dungeons & Dragons . At first, I was nonplussed by it. While the production values were impressive, it also looked like every Sony game released in the last ten years, right down to the specific angle of the camera and the quippy NPC companion. Yet as the reveal unfurled, I found myself growing intrigued by Warlock's invocation-based puzzle-solving and combat. Levitating objects to create platforms, using teleportation spells to swap places with enemies, conjuring a whole-ass storm to make electrical attacks more viable. It's rare to see a game of this scope encourage guile and cleverness from the player, to set its mechanical ambitions slightly beyond timed dodges and grisly executions. (Image credit: Wizards of the Coast) And then, just as I thought I was sold on Warlock, the main character pulled out a sword. Well, to be specific, Warlock's magical protagonist Kaatri conjured a sword. After all, why bother lugging around several pounds of sharpened steel when you can just make one appear out of thin air any time you like? It's silly to carry around a sword th…

The celebs, folks—they're just like us. More so than usual in Affleck's case, I suppose, since the actor's videogame career doesn't only encompass a brief dalliance with Blizzard's RTS series. title: Hundreds of layoffs and many cancelled projects later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma reportedly says 'we will not survive' without new IPs
summary: Having one's cake and eating it too is meant to be a metaphor.
body: Thousands of layoffs , a couple of booted studios, and a re-organisation of Obsidian away from its newer projects and onto Fallout later, Xbox CEO Asha Sharma has reportedly taken to an internal town hall and talked about the importance of new IP. The transcript, as shared by Windows Central , goes as follows: "We're backing our strongest franchises. I want our great games to become great global billion-dollar franchises. I would also like to see us continue to create enduring new IP. We will not survive if we only revive [sic] on the past. We have to find new ways, and courage, to have invention on new IP, that reaches new sets of audiences." This is, to put it gently, very confusing. As part of Xbox's "Reset", the studio has done the following: Cancelled multiple projects from Obsidian and told it to go make a Fallout game . Made Double Fine go independent . Did the same to South of Midnight studio Compulsion Games . Put its sights on Arkane Lyon . Is, at present, in consultation talks regarding Ninja Theory after attempted sales failed. That doesn't smack to me of the kind of courage and new IP invention that Sharma is talking about—most of these studios had either just made in…

title: Museum strings together 30 old Mac minis for replica of most successful supercomputer, builds something more powerful than the original
summary: Happy birthday, Apple.
body: What's better than giving the hardware you already own a fresh lease on life ? Dedicating your older tech to resurrecting even older supercomputers. At least, that's if you ask the Museo de Historia de la Computación in Spain . The hardware history museum recently used 30 Mac Minis dating between 2012 and 2014 to resurrect the Cray-1 supercomputer (via Ars Technica ). Debuting in the bygone year of 1976, the Cray-1 is noted for its striking C-shaped cabinet. However, what's arguably most impactful about the new display is that its composite parts make it technically more powerful than the original machine. The museum's exhibit features five quad-core i7s, and 25 dual-core i5s, resulting in a total of 70 cores to play with. The 30 Mac Minis run on Mojave, leveraging MacOS' Message Passing Interface to pass off computing tasks between them. When all of these cores were online during testing, the exhibit achieved 1.5 teraflops. The original Cray-1 had a 64-bit, 80 MHz processor and 8.39 MB of memory (PDF warning), with a theoretical peak performance of about 160 megaflops. It's a fitting tribute to both Apple and the Cray-1's 50th birthday this year. (Image credit: Museo de Historia …

summary: Riding the wave(guide).
body: Remember when they did motion capture on a cube ? As charming as that cutting edge cuboid is, I think VR gamers and Vtubers are gonna be all over fresh research out of MIT. Engineers at MIT have developed a sheet full of optical fibres that can digitally reconstruct its own shape even as it is flexed and folded. According to MIT News , the team reckons their tech could be fashioned into a garment that could then be used to accurately mirror your real-world movements in a game. Though currently a bulky prototype, the flexible sheet could one day be worn like a second skin that can more accurately track the transformation of a surface, rather than the movement of, say, fixed points on a traditional motion capture suit. title: The RTX 4090 launched four years ago today, and now the RTX 5090 is rumoured for the chop, I can't help but look upon it with a warm glow
summary: Times, they have a-changed.
body: Join me in saying "Happy birthday" to the RTX 4090, Nvidia's enthusiast-level graphics card of the previous generation. It launched four years ago today, October 12, with an eye-watering MSRP of $1,499. Well, eye-watering for the time. The cheapest RTX 5080 I can find right now is this Asus Prime variant for $1,640 , which is a sure sign of how things have changed in the past four years. When the second-from-top Nvidia card is now significantly more expensive than the launch MSRP of the previous generation big boi model, it's pretty easy to see how far we've fallen. And the RTX 4090's direct replacement, the RTX 5090, has reached near-unobtanium status. We've stopped tracking it on our graphics card price watch page , as the only listings around are priced at ludicrous levels from third-party sellers we're not comfortable recommending. Now rumours suggest Nvidia may have halted production of RTX 5090 chips for the consumer market , with the GB202 silicon being used for data center and professional GPUs instead. summary: I bet someone is already mocking up cat ears for this thing.
body: Valve has released the CAD files for the Steam Frame , allowing modders the perfect opportunity to get to work on their own creations for the VR headset. The light blocker—the bit that sits between the bridge of your nose and the headset—is primed for user replacement, as are the head strap, battery housing, facial interface and more. This CAD release includes the lot, along with the core module and controllers. Valve has confirmed it is working on an upgraded head strap with interchangeable batteries and off-ear speakers for the Steam Frame. That's " coming soon ". With this CAD release, perhaps we'll see more options for third parties in future, too. The docs also detail how to interface with the expansion port , or auxiliary port as Valve calls it. This sits just to the front of the user's nose and is a way for a user to add in powered accessories, ie the Arcturus Vision RGB camera—I've been playing around with that for a couple of weeks and it's a pretty wicked upgrade. title: Steam Week in Review: The curious case of Wonder Boy in Monster Land's dubious PC debut
summary: All the interesting Steam facts for the week ending October 11.
body: Wonder Boy in Monster Land released in Japanese arcades in 1987 and for the Sega Master System the following year. Its success led to numerous ports, including to ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Atari ST. Oddly, it never received an official PC port, though that long absence appeared to have come to an end on September 28. Did fans rejoice? Not really. The Steam listing for Wonderboy in Monster Land raises one immediate red flag: note the rookie error of "Wonderboy" versus Wonder Boy. The developer and publisher is Retro Maniac, whose only other Steam game is Street Hoop, or Street Slam, an old Data East arcade game from 1994. To bring you up to speed: LAT Corp owns all IP and assets once belonging to Westone Bit Entertainment, the creators of the original Wonder Boy games. But at the same time Sega, confusingly, owns the Wonder Boy trademark. In other words: LAT Corp owns the games, Sega owns the name. Both parties would need to OK any Wonder Boy re-release bearing the Wonder Boy name. Box art for Wonder Boy in Monster Land on Master System (Image credit: Sega) While the "Wonderboy" misspelling is damning, a Wonder Boy game appearing on Steam without SEGA or LAT Corp prominently di…

title: Star Wars Galactic Racer's devs tested its roguelite progression system by turning it into a board game
summary: "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system."
body: Years ago, I read that Jake Solomon prototyped the Firaxis reboot of XCOM by making a simple board game version. Something rudimentary that could be played in the office on scrap paper to get ideas across and figure out where the fun would be, without having to commit. But it's surprising to hear the same idea being used for a game as different from XCOM's turn-based tactics as Star Wars Galactic Racer. As Fuse Games' creative director Kieran Crimmins told Eurogamer , "You can't know if you can feel the system until you can play the system." And so the early prototype of this high-speed arcade racing game was indeed a board game. "You know, modern engines are so capable that you can do a lot of it in-software," CEO Matt Webster said, "but there's still something [about that which is] not as fast as getting a written idea down. From a board game perspective, you sort of decouple yourself from a particular prototype and you're talking about moment-to-moment." Specifically, the board game simulated Galactic Racer's progression system. title: Yahtzee is still out there being mean about videogames, and good for him
summary: Zero Punctuation was an essential watch back in the day. Its successor Fully Ramblomatic still carries the torch.
body: When the HMS Escapist sank everyone worth a damn swam away to form a YouTube channel called Second Wind , where Yahtzee Croshaw's video series Zero Punctuation continued under the name Fully Ramblomatic. It's not exactly the same—the people have glasses now—but it's continuing the essential work of being rude about videogames on the internet. Back in the Before Times, when someone brought a videogame magazine to school we'd all gather round to flick through it, and the only measure of whether it was a good videogame magazine was if the captions on the screenshots were funny. I didn't notice until years later, but that meant we only read the British ones. That particularly British tone is something Yahtzee's videos share. It might come across as flippant to some, but to me it's always read as deep care. Putting in the effort to make a description witty instead of plain means you're working harder to keep your audience engaged, and doing that for videogames suggests you care enough about them to want your audience to actually pay attention. Yahtzee does that. Like Blackadder finding the 100th way to tell Baldrick he's an idiot, he never runs out of ways to complain about videogames.…

title: Nier creator Yoko Taro says he's achieved his career dreams, but he continues working because it's 'good for preventing dementia'
summary: "With Drakengard, the first game I was given the opportunity to direct, I was actually able to do almost everything the way I wanted."
body: They say that art is never finished, only abandoned—but that doesn't seem to be the case for Yoko Taro, creator of Nier and Drakengard, who you might recognize by the round, smiley Emil mask he wears. According to a report from Denfaminicogamer (via IGN ), Taro said at the Tokyo French Institute last month that he's already more or less realized his vision and has considered retiring. "With Drakengard, the first game I was given the opportunity to direct, I was actually able to do almost everything the way I wanted," Taro said. "As a game otaku, I think the dream is to release something you've always wanted to create into the world. Having achieved that dream, I view everything after that as the remainder of my life." As for why he continues to work in gamedev if he's already achieved his dreams, well, he said the money doesn't hurt—and that he has a fear of how his mental health might degrade should he grow idle. "This is good for preventing dementia," he said. It's worth noting that Taro is, to put it in technical terms, a bit of a silly goose, if the mask didn't tip you off. As the IGN report notes, it's possible he doesn't literally mean that he only works in gamedev to stave …

title: RPGs are simply better when you're an idiot
summary: I just can't relate to these capable heroes.
body: Dungeon Master (Image credit: Future) Welcome to Dungeon Master , PC Gamer's regular RPG column, where Online Editor Fraser Brown delves into PC gaming's most beloved and enduring genre. Grab a seat in our badly-lit tavern and please ignore the goblin puke. Most videogame RPGs are selling a power fantasy—the idea that you are competent, clever and regardless of the odds will still manage to save the day. Fate has made you a hero, and nothing is going to stop you from achieving your goals. And this holds a lot of appeal. It's sometimes nice to be able to take a holiday from my own incompetence. Over the last few days I've managed to drop my dinner, get trapped on a bus going in the wrong direction, get peed on by a dog, get almost run over by a car and, to top it all off, actually get knocked over by an electric scooter. I am a walking disaster. (Image credit: BioWare) Geralt never gets peed on. Shepard never lands on their arse after colliding with a teen. These are not heroic moments. When these protagonists face adversity, it only serves as an excuse for more badass adventures. It turns out, though, that constantly winning becomes a little dull. I want more friction. More fuck u…

title: Escape from EloHello has me reliving my worst online PvP nightmares in roguelike-form
summary: My back hurts from carrying so hard.
body: I was stuck in elo hell for a good four years, then I entered elo purgatory for another five years, and now I'm apparently in elo heaven, but for some reason it still feels like elo hell. I guess that's just part and parcel of playing online competitive multiplayer games. While I'd never want to relive the pain of climbing from Bronze to GM, I am morbidly intrigued in whether I still have that fight in me. So I've found a happy medium, playing a strategy roguelike that provides players with "all the satisfaction of reaching rank 1, none of the toxic teammates or 40-minute hostage games". Richard Fulop Richard Fulop Richard Fulop In Escape from EloHell, you're set the task of collecting MMR as you climb the ladder from Iron 4 to Challenger, rank 1 in just 60 matches, before the season resets and you have to start again. The only way to gain MMR is to win matches, but unlike an ordinary competitive multiplayer, Escape from EloHell is a roguelike in which you have to gamble on your ability to win matches to gain effects which will help you in the long run. title: This Control-inspired action game set in a 'planet-scale alien mind' has one of the most stunning art styles I've seen this year
summary: Studio Lifeforms' Etre is shaping up to be a visual feast.
body: In the age of near photorealism, it takes a lot for a game's visuals to impress me. As cramming yet more pixels into a videogame character's face provides diminishing returns, standing out from the crowd is increasingly about how creative developers get in applying that power. All that said, I was genuinely mesmerised by the debut footage of Etre , an upcoming action adventure game with a truly eye-popping art style. Created by LA-based developer Studio Lifeforms, Etre is a narrative driven-action game set on Orbis, which Studio Lifeforms describes as a "planet-scale alien mind on the brink of awakening". You play as a character named Xyle, who arrives at this sentient cityscape in search of his soulmate Atel. According to Studio Lifeforms, the game's distinctive visuals are inspired by graphic novels of the '70s and '80s. Studio Lifeforms doesn't specify which graphics novels, and I am too much of a comics philistine to tell you. But the result is an incredibly distinctive visual style. In terms of games, Etre's closest visual cousins are the likes of Rez and Tetris Effect . But Etre applies its aesthetics to a much more grounded type of game. From a mechanical perspective, Studi…

title: Deadlock's City Never Sleeps update makes Valve's MOBA my favorite videogame setting in years
summary: I wanna be a part of it, New York, New York.
body: Play This Right Now Welcome to Play This Right Now, the site version of our weekly newsletter in which we celebrate a new game, update, or DLC that we think is well worth checking out. You can subscribe to the newsletter at the link if you want to get our thoughts about a new videogame happening direct to your inbox every Thursday. Deadlock isn't technically out yet—but it's pretty easy to get into, with invites to its beta being generously granted by Valve and obtainable in plenty of Discord communities if you don't have other mates who're into MOBA s. And boy howdy, have I not regretted a single one of my 350 hours over the past couple years "testing" this game. I've plenty of glowing words for Deadlock, but its latest update, City Never Sleeps, is like seeing one of the last few hammer-blows of a masterpiece. The entire map's been completely overhauled , with new neutral monsters and a richly-textured remake of its areas, though "remake" doesn't seem like the right word. Rather than taking what was present in the old map and scrapping it, the new Cursed Apple feels like a deepening of what was already there, adding texture and quirks in the nooks and crannies.
